Main Points
⏺ Token vesting schedules control when founders, teams, and investors can claim their tokens
⏺ Unlocks are usually spread over months or years with cliffs and linear releases
⏺ This post explains how vesting protects projects from instant dump pressure

1️⃣ What Is Vesting — tokens reserved for insiders are locked and only become claimable at set dates
2️⃣ Cliff Period — an initial lockup (for example, 6–12 months) where no tokens unlock at all
3️⃣ Linear Unlock — after the cliff, tokens are released gradually, such as monthly over several years
4️⃣ Market Impact — large unlocks can increase sell pressure, so traders often track vesting calendars
5️⃣ Trust Signal — transparent vesting shows that core contributors are aligned for the long term, not just a quick exit

Final Thoughts

Token vesting turns insider allocations into a time-based commitment — the longer they’re locked in, the more skin in the game the project really has.

Former Ethereum Foundation developer Trent Van Epps warns that Ethereum could face a funding crisis within the next 3–9 months 

For years, the Ethereum Foundation has followed a “subtraction” strategy—gradually reducing its influence so the network can thrive independently. However, EF still remains a key pillar of legitimacy through its brand, ties to Vitalik Buterin, developer events, and ecosystem coordination.

The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it.

My favorite way to work with multiple filters in pandas.Series — not a chain of .loc, but a single mask. 🐼

The chain looks neat, but breaks on real data and easily gives unexpected results:

s = pd.Series([10, 15, 20, 25, 30])
s.loc[s > 20].loc[s % 2 == 1]
The problem is that the second .loc again looks at the original s, not the already filtered result. The logic gets messy. 🤯

It's more reliable to gather everything into one expression:

s = pd.Series([10, 15, 20, 25, 30])

mask = (s > 20) & (s % 2 == 1)
result = s.loc[mask]
One mask, one point of truth. ✅

It's easier to debug. Fewer surprises when the code grows. 🚀

Bürgenstock: One Summit, Two Victories

The first high‑level US–Iran session in Bürgenstock ended exactly the way modern diplomacy likes it: with everyone declaring success in completely different languages. 

The official line from mediators Qatar and Pakistan is pure beige — “positive and constructive atmosphere,” “encouraging progress,” a political oversight committee, working groups on nuclear issues and sanctions, a 60‑day roadmap to a final deal, a de‑confliction mechanism for disputes, and a communication channel to keep Hormuz shipping “safe.” On paper, it’s process heaven.

Back home, JD Vance sells it as a macho win. He calls it “a very, very good day,” praises “very good foundations,” and brags that “yesterday there was whining” from the Iranian team, who “threatened to walk — but didn’t.” 

Then the cameras catch something else: Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif, the same mediator praising a “constructive atmosphere,” watching as the Iranian delegation actually gets up and leaves the hall in protest after Trump’s fresh threats. 

Later, Sharif still calls it “a success.” In this script, even walkouts are rebranded as progress.

Tehran’s storyline is the mirror image. Tasnim, close to the Revolutionary Guards, crows that Iran has become — “against the will of the US and Israel” — part of Lebanon’s security architecture. 

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi lists concrete gains: restrictions on oil and petrochemical exports lifted, the naval blockade removed, frozen assets being released, a reconstruction program launched. 

For him, the “first real test” isn’t nuclear transparency; it’s whether the new de‑confliction cell in Lebanon actually protects Hezbollah’s space to operate. Washington talks about mechanisms to supervise Iran. Iran talks about embedding itself inside someone else’s security system.

Neutral Switzerland does what neutral Switzerland does: blesses the progress, hopes “diplomacy will contribute to stability and peace,” and smiles for the group photo. 

China weighs in from afar to stress Iran’s “sovereignty and dignity,” because every multipolar sermon needs its applause line. And then, in a move that says more than any communiqué, the Iranian delegation flies back to Tehran the same morning — the round described as “shorter than expected” is presented as a decisive first step.

So Bürgenstock delivers two victory speeches on top of the same fragile scaffolding. One side claims it has built oversight over Iran; the other claims it has forced its way into Lebanon’s security file and traded zero core concessions for oil, cash and status. 

Between them sits the Swiss resort, a stack of committee mandates, and 60 days on the clock — with everyone agreeing only on one thing: the show must be sold as success, even when the footage shows someone walking out of the room.
